questions.prompt: What is the defining rule of structured concurrency in Swift?

options.text: A parent task cannot complete until all its child tasks have finished.
options.explanation: Structured concurrency guarantees that child tasks never outlive their parent scope.

options.text: All concurrent tasks must execute on the main thread queue.
options.explanation: Structured child tasks can execute concurrently across global thread pool executors.

options.text: Asynchronous functions must return optional values when errors occur.
options.explanation: Swift concurrency uses throwing functions and Result types, not mandatory optionals.

options.text: Tasks can only be created inside SwiftUI View body properties.
options.explanation: Structured tasks can be spawned anywhere in Swift, including models and services.

options.text: Child tasks continue running with elevated system priority levels.
options.explanation: Child tasks receive cancellation and do not elevate priority.

options.text: The operating system immediately terminates the executing POSIX thread.
options.explanation: Task cancellation in Swift is cooperative and does not kill threads.

questions.prompt: Why is task cancellation described as cooperative in Swift?

options.text: Because multiple tasks share a single thread concurrently.
options.explanation: Cooperative cancellation refers to responding to cancellation flags, not threading.

options.text: Because running tasks must inspect cancellation flags and stop voluntarily.
options.explanation: Swift does not forcibly stop tasks; tasks must check isCancelled or checkCancellation.

options.text: Because cancellation requires explicit confirmation from user interface prompts.
options.explanation: Cancellation is controlled by code logic, not UI alerts.

options.text: Because cancelled tasks donate their allocated memory to sibling tasks.
options.explanation: Memory is released when tasks deallocate through standard ARC mechanisms.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain what makes structured concurrency structured. Compare it with launching an unstructured Task { } block.

rubric.criterion: Explains the parent-child relationship where a parent task waits for all child tasks before completing
Explains automatic cancellation and priority propagation down the task tree
Contrasts with Task { } whose lifetime is not bound to the surrounding lexical scope

questions.modelAnswer: Structured concurrency organizes concurrent work into a clear parent-child tree hierarchy bound to lexical scope. A parent task cannot complete until all its child tasks have finished or cancelled. In contrast, an unstructured Task { } escapes the calling function. It continues running in the background even after the function returns.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain how withTaskGroup runs dynamic concurrent tasks. Describe how child task results are gathered by the caller.

rubric.criterion: Explains spawning child tasks dynamically inside the closure using group.addTask
Explains gathering results asynchronously using a for await loop over the task group
Mentions that withTaskGroup only returns once all child tasks finish executing

questions.modelAnswer: withTaskGroup allows developers to spawn a dynamic number of child tasks inside a closure using group.addTask. Because TaskGroup conforms to AsyncSequence, the parent collects results as they complete using for await in group. The entire withTaskGroup block suspends until all child tasks finish before returning its result.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how cancellation propagates through a structured task tree. Why must child tasks check for cancellation cooperatively?

rubric.criterion: Explains that cancelling a parent task automatically flags all child tasks as cancelled
Explains that cancellation is cooperative and does not stop threads by force
Mentions using Task.isCancelled or Task.checkCancellation() inside child tasks

questions.modelAnswer: When a parent task cancels, Swift automatically sets the cancellation flag on all child tasks in its tree. However, cancellation is cooperative, meaning the system does not forcibly terminate threads. Child tasks must periodically check Task.isCancelled or call Task.checkCancellation() to stop running early and release system resources.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, compare Task { } and Task.detached. Explain when a developer should choose Task.detached over an ordinary Task.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Task { } inherits priority, actor isolation, and task-local values from caller
Explains that Task.detached inherits nothing and runs independently on global executor
Explains choosing Task.detached for background independent work unaffected by caller actor or priority

questions.modelAnswer: An ordinary Task { } inherits the caller actor isolation, priority, and task-local values. In contrast, Task.detached runs completely independently without inheriting actor context or caller priority. Developers should pick Task.detached for heavy background computations or caching operations that should not tie to the calling actor.

questions.prompt: In 2 to 5 sentences, explain the purpose of withDiscardingTaskGroup introduced in Swift 5.9. How does it optimize memory compared to standard withTaskGroup?
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that withDiscardingTaskGroup automatically discards child task results upon completion
Explains that standard withTaskGroup retains finished results until consumed via group.next()
Identifies use cases such as long-running server loops or infinite event listeners without memory leaks

questions.modelAnswer: Standard withTaskGroup retains the result of every completed child task until it is consumed by the parent. In long-running background loops, this retained memory can grow indefinitely. withDiscardingTaskGroup automatically discards child task results immediately upon completion. This keeps memory constant for infinite producer-consumer loops.
